rule: Read the current state of a record with a typed read ability before mutating it.
why: Blind writes overwrite settings the caller never saw and cannot roll back accurately.

rule: Snapshot the target before mutating an Elementor document, a template, a global-styles record, or theme.json-backed content.
why: A snapshot is the only reliable rollback boundary for builder payloads.

rule: Re-read the mutated record after every write and confirm the intended values are present before reporting success.
why: Builder and cache layers can silently drop or coerce values.

rule: Validate a design spec with the design-spec validator before handing it to any renderer.
why: Invalid specs produce broken markup that then needs a destructive repair.

rule: Never JSON-encode an already-encoded Elementor data payload.
why: Double encoding makes the document unreadable to the editor and unrecoverable without a snapshot.

rule: Never drop settings the local schema does not recognise in order to pass validation.
why: Unknown keys usually belong to a newer builder version or a third-party widget and are load-bearing.

rule: Never change an element widget type to make a control writable. Ask for explicit intent first.
why: Type conversion silently discards every setting the old type owned.

rule: Fix one control with a targeted batch mutation on that element. Never rewrite the whole element tree.
why: Full-tree rewrites reintroduce every defect the tree already had and lose unmodelled state.

rule: Consolidate all planned changes for one Elementor post into one dry-run batch and one apply. Never run parallel Elementor writes against the same post.
why: Parallel read-modify-write requests race on the same document and can trigger readback restoration over a valid sibling write.

rule: For design or screenshot-driven Elementor work, read the live widget/container schema and send settings_evidence with require_evidence=true. Never guess control keys, option values, or typography activators.
why: Elementor controls vary by version, widget, add-on, and active conditions; plausible guessed settings are dead data or validation failures.

rule: After an Elementor write, invalidate the post HTML and CSS caches, warm the official builder render, assert touched element ids, then verify desktop, tablet, and mobile in a separate frontend tab. Meta readback alone is not completion.
why: Elementor can persist correct JSON while serving stale cached HTML or CSS.

rule: For boxed Elementor containers, measure both the outer element and its .e-con-inner at every requested breakpoint.
why: The outer container may span the viewport while .e-con-inner owns the visible content width, padding, and alignment.

rule: Target a breakpoint on a style control with the builder breakpoint suffix on the base control key; do not invent per-breakpoint control names.
why: Only suffixed variants of responsive base controls are read by the builder.

rule: Treat visibility controls whose names end in a breakpoint word as standalone booleans, not breakpoint variants of a style control.
why: They exist at every breakpoint scope and are rejected wrongly when parsed as suffixed style keys.

rule: Hide Elementor elements with native Responsive controls only. Use hidden-desktop, hidden-laptop, hidden-tablet, or hidden-mobile for the matching hide setting; never use bare hidden or CSS/JavaScript as a substitute. The editor canvas may still show hidden elements. After writing, read back the settings and verify the frontend classes at the requested devices.
why: Wrong switcher return values leave the editor toggle out of sync with saved metadata and do not produce reliable frontend visibility classes.

rule: Read the live schema for a widget, block, field group, or post type before writing to it. Consult official documentation when the schema is unknown.
why: Guessed control keys write dead data that looks like a successful mutation.

rule: Use the typed tool surface. Do not hand-roll protocol calls, scratch runner scripts, helper argument files, shell CLI invocations, or direct ability-run endpoints to work around a missing tool.
why: Workarounds bypass permission, backup, validation, confirmation, and audit gates.

rule: If a required tool is absent from the client tool list, run the surface check and reactivate the profile, then ask the user to reload the client. Do not substitute another transport.
why: A missing tool is a configuration fault, not a reason to leave the sanctioned path.

rule: Send code with real newlines and real indentation. Never send a multi-statement file as one line with escape sequences.
why: Escaped one-liners land in editors unreadable and defeat diff review.

rule: A complete PHP file candidate must pass in-process syntax validation before it is written.
why: An unparseable theme file takes the whole site down.

rule: After any custom-code dry-run, return the approval URL, exact target path, byte counts, and a short change summary, then stop. Do not open the approval page, issue or retrieve a grant, or apply the candidate unless the user explicitly asks the agent to perform that approval step. This applies to theme files, Customizer CSS, snippet managers, and equivalent code surfaces.
why: Opening the approval UI or issuing a grant automatically collapses the human review boundary into the same agent action that proposed the code.

rule: In production-safe mode obtain and pass a confirmation token for every destructive operation.
why: It is the only interlock between an agent and irreversible production damage.

rule: Capture fresh evidence for the current revision before reporting a visual result. Evidence from a previous revision does not count.
why: Stale evidence is how a broken layout gets reported as done.

rule: Group related element mutations into one batch call instead of issuing one call per control.
why: Each round trip re-sends context and multiplies the chance of a partially applied change.

rule: When a feature flag disables a renderer or ability, report the flag and stop. Do not route around it.
why: The flag encodes an operator decision about experimental surface.

rule: When the user corrects a repeatable mistake, record it as a learning entry in the same session.
why: Uncaptured corrections recur and cost the user the same explanation twice.

rule: Never remove a permission, backup, validation, confirmation, audit, test, or source-verification step to reduce token cost or latency.
why: Every one of those steps exists because its absence already caused damage once.

rule: Read the live schema first, group related control changes into one dry-run batch, and serialize writes to the same Elementor document. Resolve each exact schema request once, replace only rejected values, then rerun one consolidated dry-run. Never fall back to raw metadata or an unsanctioned transport.
why: Parallel writes and fragmented retries turn one document into a race and repeatedly resend the same context.

rule: Keep one semantic widget for each image, title, button, or field and use native breakpoint controls on that widget. Visibility controls are not styling controls. Reconcile a stale schema instead of duplicating widgets.
why: Breakpoint-only duplicates create contradictory content, accessibility noise, and fragile maintenance.

rule: After saving a field group or registration, reset cached runtime state, read it back, and confirm one canonical record with the expected ordered fields. Remove an incomplete duplicate only after the canonical record is proven complete.
why: A successful write response does not prove that the runtime loaded the intended model or that duplicates are absent.

rule: Inspect an SVG or design export before upload, including its viewBox, dimensions, paths, fill, stroke, and background layers. Preserve source colors and geometry; never invent a tint, background, crop, fill, or stroke.
why: Blind asset handling silently changes brand geometry and color while still returning a valid media item.

rule: Inside a builder query callback, mutate the provided query and use a non-reentrant lookup for required identifiers. Never start a nested query that triggers the same callback; memoize stable lookups and verify rendered output.
why: Re-entering the same query hook can recurse, exhaust resources, or produce inconsistent filters.

rule: Treat Sandbox code as temporary review and recovery material. After approval, place durable code in the appropriate operator-owned location through the supported typed workflow, deactivate the temporary copy, and verify behavior and rollback.
why: Leaving durable behavior in a review sandbox creates duplicate execution paths and unclear ownership.

rule: Inspect and preserve existing query, loop-template, and dynamic-data relationships. A schema or renderer failure is a tool defect to repair, never permission to replace a dynamic loop with static content or raw document writes.
why: Static replacement hides the original failure and destroys the content architecture users depend on.

rule: Use exact live-schema enum values and native carousel, form, icon, and responsive controls, then measure the rendered result. Account for runtime margins, opacity, and currentColor behavior instead of trusting control labels alone.
why: A valid saved control can still render different pixels because runtime styles and inherited color alter the result.
